subject: pangolin
pitch:
Category: Animal.
Subject: pangolin half curled into a ball.
Style: low-poly.
reasoning:
I'm planning the pangolin's half-curled pose—body arched in a C-shape with the head tucked low and the tail curling forward toward it, aiming for realistic proportions around 0.8m stretched, compacting down to roughly a 0.3m ball, while keeping the module reasonably sized at 500-700 lines.

Now I'm working out the spine geometry as a curved path, placing the head low near the ground facing forward and tracing how the tail wraps from the rump back around toward the front to create that curled silhouette.

For the body shape itself, I'm thinking of sweeping an elliptical cross-section along the spine chain, with the hips as a root joint and the tail curling off to the side so it doesn't intersect the legs.

Now I'm mapping out the actual spine curve points from hips to head, then sketching a small cone-shaped head angled forward and down from the neck.

I need to make sure the belly stays clear of the ground given short pangolin-style legs, so I'm checking radius values against leg length to keep the proportions physically plausible—aiming for a total body height around 0.33 units.

Redefining the spine chain points from tail to head with positions and radii, then adjusting the radius-interpolation function along the sweep to taper smoothly from tail tip through the widest torso section down to the narrower neck and head base.

For the scales, I'm thinking through how to achieve the pangolin's signature overlapping-plate look efficiently -- rows of flattened low-poly cone shapes stuck onto the body surface, keeping triangle and part counts within budget by limiting each scale's geometry.

I need each scale to orient with its flat face pointing outward and its tip aimed rearward along the spine, so I'm working out the flow direction as the negative tangent since the spine path runs hip-to-head. For the actual scale shape, I'm considering a flattened cone geometry scaled into a diamond-like plate to mimic shingled scales.

Figuring out cone vertex orientation...

For flow direction, I'll pass the reversed tangent for spine orientation, with scales pointing toward the tip along the spine. For coloring, I'll skip per-part paints and just use flat colors from a small palette of browns and olives chosen randomly to keep things performant.

Now I'm figuring out the gradient scheme - lighter warm tan on top, darker olive-brown on the sides, darkest below, with a few shade variants per zone for natural variation. I'm also sizing out the scale rows along the body length and circumference, landing on roughly 14 staggered rows of about 9 scales each, overlapping at half-offset, for around 110 scales total.

For the tail I'm planning roughly 12 rows of 6 scales. The legs get scales on their outer surface but soft skin inside, the small head has scales on top with soft pinkish-gray skin on the face, and the neck stays skin-colored. I'm defining the belly as a pale pinkish-grey sector against the darker brown scale base, mapped onto the body sweep so the belly sits along the inside of the curled pose. Now I'm shaping the head as an elongated, conical form with small eyes and barely-there ear nubs, joining it at the neck.

Shaping snout, jaw, eyes and nose with low-poly sweeps...

I'm weighing whether to just stick simple bulge spheres for eyes and decal the iris texture onto them, rather than overcomplicating with surface hit calculations—deciding to keep it simpler by bulging then decaling.

I'll build the eye texture with a darker lid ring, dark pupil, highlight, and transparent edges, then decal it onto the head sweep surface for each eye. Now I'm working out the head joint geometry—positioning the head base and figuring the slant direction toward the snout tip so the eyes land correctly on the sides.

Adjusting the tilt so the nose doesn't sink too close to the floor, I'm recalculating the head's base and tip coordinates and setting up radii that taper from base to tip, then defining the sweep path connecting those points.

Now I'm sketching out the skeleton hierarchy — placing the hips as the root joint, building a spine chain through catmull-rom control points, and figuring out how to name each spine segment so the head attaches cleanly as a child of the chain.

I'm sweeping a single body tube using a bone list of [spine, neck] for smooth bending, with the body path built as a catmull curve through all the joint points so the mesh follows the chain naturally.

The head sweep overlaps the body end with distinct coloring to distinguish skin from scales. For legs, I'm working out the pangolin's limb structure—forelegs with curved claws, shorter plantigrade hind legs—using IK with shoulder joints positioned on the body underside and foot targets defined for the tucked half-curl pose.

I'm computing the arm chain: a two-segment limb bending the elbow backward, with shoulder-to-foot distance of 0.121 fitting within the 0.14 combined segment length, then adding a flat hand shape with three claw spikes at the wrist.

Positioning the claw spikes...

Now working through the hind legs: hip at the back, knee bending forward, ankle back, with foot targets near the ground so the leg chain lands correctly. I'm setting plantigrade feet where the sole extends forward from the heel, making sure the ankle sits at ground level with the foot capsule running toward the front.

I'm checking that the tail, which runs from the rump backward, doesn't overlap the hind legs. For the legs themselves, I'm sweeping a tapered tube from thigh to ankle with thicker radius near the hip, using a soft grey-brown skin tone, and considering adding a few scales along the outer thigh for texture.

Writing scale paint logic...

Now I'm sketching the tail's path in plan view, defining the base-to-tip curve with waypoints sweeping from the body around the left side, and tracking how its height tapers along the way.

I'm working out the tail's radius profile, making sure the taper from base to tip stays consistent with the dropping y-height so the shape sinks correctly without the bottom clipping below center.

Checking clearance between the tail tip and the foreleg hand position, it looks like there's enough separation in both x and z so they won't overlap.

Now I'm setting up the tail as a chain of 7 bones parented to the hips, starting near the tail base, which sits close to where the body ends — I want to confirm the attachment point lines up reasonably with the body radius there.

I'm figuring out how to place keeled scale rows along the tail's sweep path, covering most of the circumference except the underside near the ground, with scale size shrinking in proportion to the tail's tapering radius.

Writing scale placement function...

Still working out scale distribution...

Without rotation I'll keep flat plates but make overlaps real by setting plate length longer than row spacing, so neighboring scales geometrically cross rather than z-fight. I'm considering whether to bury the front edge and raise the rear tip for a true shingled look, though that'd require custom geometry rather than a simple cone.

Let me reconsider the orientation — flipping the apex to point forward (buried) with the pentagon base raised at the rear gives a raised trailing edge, which better matches how overlapping scales actually sit, with a slightly flattened disc shape for the exposed flap.

Confirms the pentagon vertex points up, giving the wedge shape I want. I'm setting the scale dimensions for width, base height, and length, with the geometry centered at y=0 so it embeds naturally into the surface, half above and half below.

Flow direction should point toward the rear on the body (toward the head via tangent) and toward the tip on the tail, matching how real pangolin scales overlap with free edges pointing tailward. I'll pass the negated tangent vector as the flow array, keep colors shared per part, and figure out triangle counts for the cone geometry with caps.

With roughly 300 total parts across body, tail, and legs, triangle counts stay manageable, and I'll use faceted (flat) normals for a scaly look. I'm considering adding finer scatter scales on the head top and neck for extra detail.

I'm thinking through the dorsal spine and keeled rows but deciding to skip extra ridges for simplicity, and planning the tail's underside angle range since it stays curled. I'm setting up base skin coloring and a belly sector with a lighter tone, defining the angular range for where that skin patch shows through the scales, then moving on to eyes and ears.

For the ears, I'm adding tiny skin flaps as small bumps, and giving the nose a dark flattened bulb with tiny nostril spheres. I'm giving the head a countershaded skin tone, darker tan on top and lighter near the belly, then scaling down the tiny head scales proportionally to the head's radius.

For scale spacing, I'm computing row counts by dividing the sweep's arc length by a fixed step distance, pulling that length from the sweep curve rather than guessing, then mapping t values across the head and tail accordingly.

Now I'm sketching the eye texture design — small, dark, drooping eyes set against a skin-toned lid ring, matching the heavy-lidded look of a real pangolin's face. Writing SVG code...

Working out the decal placement for the eyes using surface sampling around the head center, figuring out the azimuth and elevation angles that position them symmetrically on the sides near the front of the cranium.

With the shoulder joint confirmed just barely inside the body ellipse, I'm plotting the foreleg path from shoulder to elbow to hand, then nudging the hand's x-position further outward so the legs read clearly as visible limbs rather than tucking invisibly under the body.

Now I'm working out the hand: positioning the wrist and hand capsule, then adding three cream-colored claws angled forward and slightly curved downward, checking that their bottoms stay above ground level. I'm noting that the limbs look sufficiently separated and extended, and starting to think about how to assign rig roles like "leg" to the joint chains.

For the rig, I'm deciding forelimbs should use the "arm" role while hindlimbs keep "leg," with jaw and head getting their own labeled joints. I'm also sketching out a warm tan color palette for the dorsal scales, starting with top and mid-tone hex values.

Mid-tone and lower scale shades, body base, belly skin, face countershading, nose, claw, and eye colors are getting finalized, and I'm checking that all ground-contact points like hands, feet, and tail rest properly at y=0.
